Organization and Nature of Business
NanoViricides, Inc. (the “Company”, “NanoViricides”, “we,” or “us”) was incorporated in Nevada on April 1, 2005, and redomiciled to Delaware effective May 30, 2023. Our corporate offices are located at 1 Controls Drive, Shelton, Connecticut 06484 and our telephone number is (203) 937-6137. Our Website is located at http://www.Nanoviricides.com . We do not incorporate by reference into this Annual Report the information on or accessible through our website, and you should not consider it part of this Annual Report.
On September 25, 2013, the Company’s common stock began trading on the New York Stock Exchange American under the symbol, “NNVC”.
We are a clinical stage company. Phase II clinical trials of our first drug, NV-387, has previously successfully completed a Phase Ia/Ib clinical trial for human clinical safety and tolerability, wherein the drug was found to be safe and well tolerated, with no reportable adverse events, and no subjects dropping out.. Additionally, drug candidates in various stages of pre-clinical development, including IND-filing stage and late stage IND-enabling non-clinical studies. We have no customers, products or revenues to date, and may never achieve revenues or profitable operations.
We are engaged in developing a class of drugs, that we call nanoviricides™, using a platform technology based on the application of nanomedicine technologies to the complex issues of viral diseases. This approach enables rapid development of effective new drugs against a number of different viruses, that the viruses are highly unlikely to escape even as they evolve rapidly in the field, solving an important problem in attacking viruses. In contrast, viruses readily escape vaccines, antibodies and small chemical drugs developed using the traditional antiviral approaches because, generally speaking, a small number of mutations allow the virus to become resistant, and thereupon resistant viruses can continue to grow and expand.

NanoViricides Technology Platform Target Product Profile in Brief
We are a clinical stage company developing (a) host-mimetic, and (b) direct-acting, nanomachines capable of dismantling a targeted virus, (c) without assistance from the human immune system.
a.
Virus Escape Unlikely-As a host-mimetic, viruses cannot escape a nanoviricide drug by generating mutants and variants in the field, because all variants still require the same signature host features that our drugs mimic. In contrast, vaccines, antibodies and small chemical drugs are readily escaped by viruses as mutations occur, rendering these medical countermeasures ineffective.
b.
Direct Antivirals Expected to Provide Significant Safety and Tolerability Benefits- As a direct-acting antiviral, a nanoviricide drug is not expected to interfere with human bodily systems or enzymes, which is expected to result in significant levels of safety, unlike most of the antiviral drugs that interfere with cellular processes.
c.
Applicable for All Patient Population- As a complete nanomachine that is designed to bind, engulf, and destroy virus particles without dependence on the patient’s physiology, a nanoviricide is expected to provide antiviral effect for all patients, from infants, pediatrics, adults, to seniors.
d.
Does Not Require Healthy Immune System-Any viral infection that causes significant pathology does so by virtue of host immune system disrepair, either pre-existing, or caused by the virus itself. Therefore, nanoviricides can be expected to be superior to approaches such as vaccines and antibodies that require a good functional host immune system for antiviral response.
These distinctive features that set nanoviricides apart from the entire world of current antiviral approaches are made possible by our novel nanoviricide chemical nanomachine design. After decades of development, this novel nanoviricide technology has now successfully reached clinical stage and regulatory processes towards approval of drugs for commercialization.
NV-387, Phase II Clinical Trials; Regulatory Developments
Our first clinical stage drug candidate, NV-387, has completed Phase Ia/Ib human clinical trial for the evaluation of safety and tolerability in healthy subjects. NV-387 is the active ingredient in the two drug product formulations labeled “NV-CoV-2 Oral Syrup” and “NV-CoV-2 Oral Gummies” that we developed for the treatment of COVID infection. In this clinical trial for safety and tolerability in healthy human adult subjects: (a) there were no drop-outs, (b) there were no reported adverse events, and (c) the drugs were well-tolerated even at the highest level of dosing given multiple times. These results are indicative of safety and tolerability that have been successfully achieved for NV-387. The final Phase I Clinical Study Report is completed by the CRO. We expect its submission soon. The final report submission was delayed because of the workload for the purpose of initiating the Phase II clinical trial of NV-387 Oral Gummies for the Treatment of Ebola virus during the current, worst-ever Ebola Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). A Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) for Ebola was declared by the WHO on May 17, 2026.
Two Phase II clinical trials, (i) NV-387 Oral Gummies for the Treatment of Mpox (Monkeypox) and (ii) NV-387 Oral Gummies for the Treatment of Ebola are about to start in the DRC; both under respective regulatory approvals from the local agency, Autorité Congolaise de Réglementation Pharmaceutique (“ACOREP”).
Additionally, (iii) The Viral ARI clinical trial will provide information on the effectiveness of NV-387 treatment on a number of viral infections including Influenzas, RSV, Coronaviruses, hMPV, and others, in a single clinical trial.
If successful, the Viral ARI and Viral SARI clinical trials could lead to NV-387 becoming the world’s first empiric antiviral treatment, i.e. a broad-spectrum antiviral that a physician could prescribe at first visit, akin to how bacterial infections are treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, after regulatory approvals.
If the Measles program is successful, the Company would be eligible for a Priority Review Voucher (PRV) from the US FDA. Recently, PRVs have been sold for about $200-220 million 1 . A PRV, if issued to us, and sold by us, could bring cash to the Company even prior to revenues from commercialization of a drug.

The Company also intends to bring its Mpox (aka Monkeypox) and Ebola clinical trials programs under respective US FDA INDs. The Company intends to seek appropriate meetings to seek advice for these purposes with the US FDA soon.
The Orphan Drug Designation (“ODD”) will qualify NanoViricides for incentives according to the US FDA 1 that include: tax credits for qualified clinical trials; exemption from certain FDA user fees; as well as potential seven years of market exclusivity after approval.
The Rare Paediatric Disease Designation (“RPDD”) designation enables that a Priority Review Voucher (PRV) can be issued to the Company upon a successful Marketing Application (i.e. New Drug Application) for the use of NV-387 as a treatment for Measles, provided all of the required conditions are met. The Company can use the PRV, if granted, to reduce review times on another of its drug applications. Importantly, a PRV can be sold to another Pharmaceutical Company for accelerating their drug program as well, which provides a high value to the purchaser. Recently, PRVs have been sold for $200-220 Million dollars each 2 .
NV-387 is a uniquely broad-spectrum antiviral drug that has demonstrated strong activity in lethal lung infection animal modelstudies Coronaviruses, RSV, Influenzas, Measles (in a humanized mice model), all of which are distinctly different RNA viruses. In addition, NV-387 has also demonstrated strong activity in a orthopoxvirus, that are DNA viruses.
These distinct types of viruses share a common feature; that they all utilize heparan sulfate proteoglycan (HSPG) or related Sulfated Proteoglycans (S-PG) as the first “attachment receptor” to which they bind and thereby prepare to attack the cells and cause infection. This initial step leads to the virus particles congregating on the cell surface. Some of these particles may then be able to bind to another cell-surface receptor(s). called the “cognate receptor(s)”. Upon binding to the cognate receptor, the virus particle fuses with the cell and enters the cell initiating a cascade of steps involving dismantling, making copies of itself, assembling, and exiting out of the cell.
